title: Using labour-market information
objective: I can use current data on opportunities, skills demand, pay or growth to draw a cautious conclusion about a career area.
objective_verbatim: I can use current data on opportunities, skills demand, pay or growth to draw a cautious conclusion about a career area.
display_objective: I can use current data on opportunities, skills demand, pay or growth to draw a cautious conclusion about a career area.
weekly_outcome: Students interpret current LMI to inform, rather than dictate, career decisions.
subject: Careers

source_adaptation: All labour-market figures are invented inside this pack as required. The exact scheme outcome remains unchanged. The named-area/current-data activity in H10 is replaced by generic practice sets A and B. Use the latest window within the fictional set, while teaching how a real source date would be checked. This lesson evidences interpretation and caution with illustrative data; it does not demonstrate use of verified current real-world labour-market data. Record that boundary rather than claiming full real-data application.
success: Identify practice source, report date, period and unit.
Use an accurate value or comparison to support a conclusion.
Give a relevant limit and one next research question.
threads: Thread tags: SMSC S/So (M/C: none); British Values IL/MR (D/RL/T: none).
prepare: Books, pens, the two practice data sheets, vocabulary mat and normal reading or typing aids. Offer one print set per learner. Use an adult model before the independent task. No web access, login or pupil phone is needed. A calculator is normal access if useful.
activity: Retrieve sector and occupation; model source/date/unit checks; compare A and test forecast B; independently analyse one sector in one set; give feedback, fade answer prompts, reflect and retain actual work.

evidence.description: An individual LMI analysis with source/date, period/unit, accurate supporting data, a cautious conclusion, a relevant limit and one next research question. Retain actual support and any revision.

evidence_detail: An individual LMI analysis with source/date, period/unit, accurate supporting data, a cautious conclusion, a relevant limit and one next research question. Retain actual support and any revision.
assessment: The source marks this week formative. Retain the learner’s first claim, data reference, relevant limit, next question, actual support and any revision. Accurate interpretation of the supplied practice set is valid lesson evidence. Do not claim that illustrative figures demonstrate current real-world labour-market conditions. Any later real-source application needs a fresh, checked source and a separate record.
boundaries: No actual labour-market fact, wage claim, real region, employer, organisation or entry requirement appears in the practice sets. Do not ask about household income or employment. Avoid ranking sectors or learners by worth. Data may guide inquiry, but interests, values, access and wider evidence also matter. No final career decision is required. Follow the usual safeguarding route if a concern arises.
feedback: VF verbal feedback; WS worked with support; I independent; NS next step; // self-edit; ? read this back to me; E evidence recorded; R responded. Give one precise next step linked to the number, source or limit. R requires Voice and Audience, the NS and a learner response in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode. A private adult may be the audience. Use E only when actual evidence is banked.
response_modes: Work in the book by default. Type instead is an optional equivalent response area with the same fields and demand. No pupil phone or login is required. Keep reader, scribe, normal aid and typing as access, not a lower route.

routes.Independent: Use the structured record to choose A or B, read the units and dates, justify a cautious conclusion with accurate data and give a next research question. A comparison within one source is enough. No compulsory personal career disclosure or public answer.
routes.Supported: Use one source and one row at a time. Provide the vocabulary bank, a separate worked example and short prompts. Highlight the source/date strip and column labels. Cover unneeded rows. Keep the evidence demand: accurate data, source/date and a bounded conclusion. Fade answer scaffolds where secure.
routes.Floor: Use source A, the retail row and the printed choices. Learner selects the right numbers, chooses or states a cautious conclusion, and points to source/date. An adult can read and record the learner’s choice. Keep a relevant limit and next question through speech, pointing or typing. Record which elements were demonstrated and any supplied answers; do not claim a copied model as independent work.

adaptations.Cognition and Learning: Use explicit teaching, a separate model and guided practice. Chunk the table by source and row. Keep the unit beside each number. Use the same short check routine for both sets. Offer a simple record structure and extra processing time.
adaptations.Communication and Interaction: Pre-teach source, date, advert and forecast. Rehearse a sentence privately. Accept speech, pointing, reader, scribe or typing. Use short questions and allow wait time. No cold calling or forced pair work.
adaptations.SEMH: Predictable five-phase sequence and private feedback. Use neutral sectors; no family income, job loss or personal future disclosure. Offer a regulation break and a planned return. “Not sure yet” can lead to a specific next question.
adaptations.Sensory and Physical: Offer large print, one-row view and the usual reading or input aid. Avoid colour-only cues. Learners may use a calculator, scribe or keyboard. Keep the space calm and uncluttered.
adaptations.EAL: Plan in any language. Check the meaning of count, latest and forecast with an example. Offer oral rehearsal and the same source labels. Treat language access separately from evidence of reasoning.

hinge: Source A has 24 retail adverts in October. Which claim fits? A: Everyone can get a retail job. B: This practice set counted 24 retail adverts in that window. Answer B. Ask for the number and a limit. If the learner selects A or cannot explain the unit, re-model the difference between an advert count and a personal job guarantee. Recheck privately before independent work.
parallel_hinge: Source B predicts 104 construction posts for October 2027 if the plans stay the same. Which claim fits? A: The model suggests 104 posts if its plan holds. B: There are 104 jobs to apply for today. Answer A. If uncertain, label the future date and the assumption. Retain a supported path and log partial evidence if the distinction remains insecure.
prompt_ladder: 1. Point to the place or instruction. 2. Ask a short question. 3. Rephrase the instruction. 4. Provide a scaffold or choice. 5. Model the first step only, then return the task.
frames: F: “Source ... is dated ... . It counts ... . The number is ... .” M: “In this set, ... changes from ... to ... . This may suggest ... .” H: “This conclusion is limited because ... . I would check ... before using it for a real choice.”
misconceptions: “More adverts means I will get a job.” An advert count is only one clue. It does not show an individual chance, all vacancies, or who was hired. “A forecast is a fact about next year.” It is a prediction based on assumptions. Plans and conditions can change.
ta_focus: I do: check the learner can find the source/date and unit. We do: prompt a number or label as evidence; do not select the claim for the learner. Independent: log access and actual answer prompts, then fade support when secure. Support a calm return after a break.

Practice_A.label: Practice source A
Practice_A.unit: advert records counted in the same fictional collection, per 28-day window
Practice_A.method: One count per advert record in each window. The collection is not a complete labour-market census. An advert count is not a count of people hired.
limits: Advert counts do not show all jobs or a person’s chance of getting one.
Two short periods do not establish a lasting trend.

Practice_B.label: Practice source B
Practice_B.unit: total posts in a different fictional collection, starting at 100 posts per sector
Practice_B.method: Conditional planning model. The starting counts are made-up baselines. Future counts are predictions, not observations.
Practice_B.assumption: Assume the made-up service and spending plans stay the same. If plans change, the forecast can change.
limits: Predicted posts are not current vacancies.
The forecast is conditional and cannot guarantee a job.
A and B count different things, so do not add or compare their raw totals.

accreditation: Staff confirm any accredited mapping from actual work. No criteria or unit completion inferred.

paragraphs_in_document_order: Tuesday 10 November 2026 · P3 · 40 minutes · Year A
GROW · up to five learners · Independent is the default
Unit: Identity & Belonging — Belonging in work
Thread tags: SMSC S/So (M/C: none); British Values IL/MR (D/RL/T: none).
I can use current data on opportunities, skills demand, pay or growth to draw a cautious conclusion about a career area.
Weekly outcome: Students interpret current LMI to inform, rather than dictate, career decisions.

Source: specialist Careers scheme, GROW Careers, physical row 10, Autumn 2 row 2. Focus F10; outcome G10; sequence H10; timing I10; evidence J10; access K10; support L10; end check M10; formative N10.
What can a table about work tell us, and what does it leave out?
1. Identify the practice source, report date, time window and unit. 2. Use an accurate value or comparison to support a conclusion. 3. Give a relevant limit and one next research question.

Books, pens, the two practice data sheets, vocabulary mat and normal reading or typing aids. Offer one print set per learner. Use an adult model before the independent task. No web access, login or pupil phone is needed. A calculator is normal access if useful.

All labour-market figures are invented inside this pack as required. The exact scheme outcome remains unchanged. The named-area/current-data activity in H10 is replaced by generic practice sets A and B. Use the latest window within the fictional set, while teaching how a real source date would be checked. This lesson evidences interpretation and caution with illustrative data; it does not demonstrate use of verified current real-world labour-market data. Record that boundary rather than claiming full real-data application.
This helps me weigh evidence about work and choose what to research next. Work data can guide a question without deciding a learner’s future.
Recall sector and occupation from Week 1. Offer retail and checkout work as a neutral example. Ask what numbers about work might help us find out.
Introduce LMI and the practice-data label. Model source, report date, observation window and unit with source A. Read one pair of values and form a limited claim.
Compare construction and retail in A. Discuss the different units and the conditional forecast in B. Use the private hinge and parallel hinge.
Choose one sector in A or B. Record source/date/window/unit, a value or comparison, a cautious conclusion, a limit and one next question. Give feedback, then fade answer prompts.
Check whether the conclusion follows from the data without overclaiming. Learner revises or explains their thinking. Keep actual evidence and a next question in the Careers Portfolio/action plan.
The five phases total 40 minutes. Vocabulary, checks, feedback and access pauses sit within these phases. Slide 11 can be used when needed; slide 12 is a hidden staff reference.

Model source A, health and care: “Practice source A, fictional report date 2 November 2026. It counts advert records in two 28-day windows. The count goes from 12 in September to 18 in October. That is six more records. In this set, more care adverts were counted in October. This does not prove that every care job is easy to get. I would next check what skills the roles ask for.” Read the source/date aloud. The report is fictional.
Fade to construction: prompt source/date, then ask for 20 and 24. Next, let the learner choose a row without the model. Retain normal reading or scribing access.

Ask privately: What is counted: advert records or people hired? Which label gives the period counted, rather than the report date? If either is unclear, point to the table header and model one row again before moving on.

Use the structured record to choose A or B, read the units and dates, justify a cautious conclusion with accurate data and give a next research question. A comparison within one source is enough. No compulsory personal career disclosure or public answer.

Use one source and one row at a time. Provide the vocabulary bank, a separate worked example and short prompts. Highlight the source/date strip and column labels. Cover unneeded rows. Keep the evidence demand: accurate data, source/date and a bounded conclusion. Fade answer scaffolds where secure.

Use source A, the retail row and the printed choices. Learner selects the right numbers, chooses or states a cautious conclusion, and points to source/date. An adult can read and record the learner’s choice. Keep a relevant limit and next question through speech, pointing or typing. Record which elements were demonstrated and any supplied answers; do not claim a copied model as independent work.

Use explicit teaching, a separate model and guided practice. Chunk the table by source and row. Keep the unit beside each number. Use the same short check routine for both sets. Offer a simple record structure and extra processing time.

Pre-teach source, date, advert and forecast. Rehearse a sentence privately. Accept speech, pointing, reader, scribe or typing. Use short questions and allow wait time. No cold calling or forced pair work.

Predictable five-phase sequence and private feedback. Use neutral sectors; no family income, job loss or personal future disclosure. Offer a regulation break and a planned return. “Not sure yet” can lead to a specific next question.
Offer large print, one-row view and the usual reading or input aid. Avoid colour-only cues. Learners may use a calculator, scribe or keyboard. Keep the space calm and uncluttered.
Plan in any language. Check the meaning of count, latest and forecast with an example. Offer oral rehearsal and the same source labels. Treat language access separately from evidence of reasoning.
Normal reader/scribe/typing, aids and processing time do not automatically change the academic route. Record access mode separately from answer prompts.

Source A has 24 retail adverts in October. Which claim fits? A: Everyone can get a retail job. B: This practice set counted 24 retail adverts in that window. Answer B. Ask for the number and a limit. If the learner selects A or cannot explain the unit, re-model the difference between an advert count and a personal job guarantee. Recheck privately before independent work.

Source B predicts 104 construction posts for October 2027 if the plans stay the same. Which claim fits? A: The model suggests 104 posts if its plan holds. B: There are 104 jobs to apply for today. Answer A. If uncertain, label the future date and the assumption. Retain a supported path and log partial evidence if the distinction remains insecure.

F: “Source ... is dated ... . It counts ... . The number is ... .” M: “In this set, ... changes from ... to ... . This may suggest ... .” H: “This conclusion is limited because ... . I would check ... before using it for a real choice.”

I do: check the learner can find the source/date and unit. We do: prompt a number or label as evidence; do not select the claim for the learner. Independent: log access and actual answer prompts, then fade support when secure. Support a calm return after a break.
1. Point to the place or instruction. 2. Ask a short question. 3. Rephrase the instruction. 4. Provide a scaffold or choice. 5. Model the first step only, then return the task.

“More adverts means I will get a job.” An advert count is only one clue. It does not show an individual chance, all vacancies, or who was hired. “A forecast is a fact about next year.” It is a prediction based on assumptions. Plans and conditions can change.

Evidence J10: LMI analysis with source/date and cautious conclusion. End check M10: Can the student make a conclusion that is supported by the data without overclaiming? Use the learner’s own response. Check the number, unit and period; a cautious word alone does not fix an unsupported claim.

The source marks this week formative. Retain the learner’s first claim, data reference, relevant limit, next question, actual support and any revision. Accurate interpretation of the supplied practice set is valid lesson evidence. Do not claim that illustrative figures demonstrate current real-world labour-market conditions. Any later real-source application needs a fresh, checked source and a separate record.

Work in the book by default. Type instead is an optional equivalent response area with the same fields and demand. No pupil phone or login is required. Keep reader, scribe, normal aid and typing as access, not a lower route.

VF verbal feedback; WS worked with support; I independent; NS next step; // self-edit; ? read this back to me; E evidence recorded; R responded. Give one precise next step linked to the number, source or limit. R requires Voice and Audience, the NS and a learner response in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode. A private adult may be the audience. Use E only when actual evidence is banked.

Keep the analysis in the Careers Portfolio or action plan under usual arrangements. Offer one genuine explanation to the Communication portfolio; staff confirm any mapping. No unit completion is inferred. Never bank a blank record or the staff model as learner evidence.
Teaching need next lesson ____________________ Learner next research question ____________________

No actual labour-market fact, wage claim, real region, employer, organisation or entry requirement appears in the practice sets. Do not ask about household income or employment. Avoid ranking sectors or learners by worth. Data may guide inquiry, but interests, values, access and wider evidence also matter. No final career decision is required. Follow the usual safeguarding route if a concern arises.

Year A. Autumn 2 Week 2, 9–13 November 2026. One lesson on Tuesday 10 November, P3, 40 minutes. Week 7 is assessing; Week 6 retains its mixed formative/summative source role. Week 3 follows only after this return is downloaded.

Autumn 2 Week 2 · 9–13 November 2026 · Tuesday 10 November · P3

GROW Careers, physical row 10 / Autumn 2 row 2; E10–N10

Recall sector/occupation. Model source/date/unit checks with A. Compare table values and a conditional forecast. Individually use one practice set to draw a cautious conclusion, give a limit and a next research question. Give feedback, fade answer prompts and reflect.
An individual LMI analysis with source/date and cautious conclusion, accurate supporting data, a relevant limit and next question.
Can the student make a conclusion that is supported by the data without overclaiming?
Independent / Supported / Floor. Reader, scribe and typing normal. No cold calling. Record answer prompts separately.

Formative. The figures are illustrative and generic, by owner instruction. They replace the named-area/live-data activity. Keep the exact outcome, but record this lesson as practice in interpreting evidence and making cautious claims. Current real-world data use is not evidenced by these invented sets. Week 6 retains mixed source assessment; Week 7 is assessing.
This helps me weigh evidence about work and choose what to research next.

Pre-teach the vocabulary, model one row, use guided comparison and a structured record. Offer one-row view, extra processing, usual aids and a regulation break. Plan in any language and rehearse privately. No personal income or career disclosure is required.

Keep source/date, period/unit, accurate number or comparison, cautious claim, relevant limit and next question. Retain first thinking and any change. Offer to the Communication portfolio. Use E only for actual banked evidence. Give one NS and use R only after Voice, Audience and the learner’s response.

Year A. Autumn 2 Week 2. Tuesday 10 November 2026 P3. One 40-minute lesson. No clock time supplied.
Adult record. Use the book or Type instead. Keep the learner’s own words. They may read, point, speak, type or use a scribe.
Learner code __________ Actual date __________ Route __________ Work reference __________
Usual way to work ____________________ Help with an answer ____________________
Time window and what is counted
Keep the first claim and any change. These are made-up data. Do not record them as real work facts.
One NS ____________________ Learner response in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode ____________________
Voice and Audience present ______ Response date ______ R after NS and response ______ Evidence banked ______
Careers · GROW · Autumn 2 · Week 02 · CAREERS-GROW-A2-W02 · Date __________
Today I can: □ find source and date □ use a number to back a view □ say what the data cannot show
In your book: record one source, its date, the unit and period. Use a number to support a cautious claim. Give a limit and a next question. Offer to the Communication portfolio.
Type here instead of your book if you choose. The task stays the same. You may use a reader, scribe, speech, pointing or your usual aid.
Report date ____________________ Period or future date ____________________
Before a real choice, I would check _________________________________________
Usual way to work / help with an answer ____________________________________
These figures are made up for practice. They cannot tell me the real job market.
Illustrative practice data. All figures and report dates are made up. They do not describe real work or real places.
The precise outcome is retained: I can use current data on opportunities, skills demand, pay or growth to draw a cautious conclusion about a career area.

Use the fictional report date of 2 November 2026 to practise provenance checks. Distinguish it from the periods in the column headers. These sources have no real region, organisation or employer. The task does not evidence actual current labour-market conditions.

Source A counts advert records in the same fictional collection over 1–28 September and 1–28 October 2026. Both windows last 28 days. The collection is not complete. Counts are not people hired, all jobs or a person’s chance of selection.

Model answer: “Source A, fictional report date 2 November 2026, shows construction advert records rose from 20 to 24 between the two 28-day windows. This suggests four more records in this set. It does not prove a lasting trend or guarantee a job. I would next check the tasks and skills in those adverts.”

Retail and construction both have 24 in October. Their changes differ: retail fell from 30; construction rose from 20. A latest count and a change answer different questions. Avoid calling either sector best.

Source B, fictional report date 2 November 2026, uses invented October 2026 starting counts and October 2027 predictions for total posts in a different collection. Every sector starts at 100 for teaching simplicity. Posts may be occupied. The table does not count vacancies or jobs to apply for.
The conditional assumption is that the made-up service and spending plans stay the same. A plan change could change the result. The forecast is not an observed future fact.

Model answer: “In source B, the construction forecast is 104 total posts for October 2027, from a made-up baseline of 100. The model suggests four more posts if its plans hold. This is uncertain and does not mean 104 vacancies today. I would ask what evidence and assumptions support the forecast before applying it to a real choice.”

A and B have different units and collections. Do not combine counts, calculate a vacancy rate from them, or use B to prove A. Either source can support the independent task when the learner states its unit and limit. Calculating differences is helpful but not mandatory; accurate direct values also support a conclusion.
Retail is a sector. Checkout assistant is an occupation. If Week 1 was missed, supply this neutral example without marking prior completion. Invite a question about numbers, tasks or skills.
The unit in A is advert records, not people hired. The report date is 2 November; the two counting windows appear in the column headers. Re-model these labels if needed.

Main hinge: B is correct. Source A counted 24 retail adverts in its October window; it cannot show everyone can get a retail job. Ask for evidence and a limit. If incorrect or unsupported, point to the unit and re-model before independent work.

Parallel hinge: A is correct. Source B suggests 104 construction posts in October 2027 if its plans hold; it does not show 104 jobs available today. Revisit future date and assumption if needed. Record unresolved uncertainty and the chosen support.

Ask: What is the source label? Is its report date the same as its data period? What is counted? Is the future number observed or predicted? What does the source leave out? In a real inquiry, check who produced the data, method, coverage, update date and fit to the question. A recent date alone does not establish trustworthiness.

“More adverts means I will get a job.” Correct with the limits of advert counts and personal selection. “Forecasts are facts.” Correct with the assumptions and future date. The word “may” alone cannot rescue a claim contradicted by the table.

Keep the separate model, source strips, vocabulary bank and one-row view. Floor key is A, B, A, A, B, A. Accept speaking or pointing with a faithful scribe. Record the learner’s own selections before any explanation that supplies an answer.

Source J10 calls for LMI analysis with source/date and cautious conclusion. Collect one individual response with accurate data, unit/period, a claim that follows, a relevant limit and one implication for further research. Record missing elements separately. Do not require all four sectors or all types of LMI; the source outcome uses opportunities, skills demand, pay or growth.

Secure practice: “In A, retail goes from 30 to 24 adverts. That is fewer in the later window. It does not show all retail work. I would check the skills asked for.” Source/report date and periods should be present in the record or clearly pointed to. Partial: a correct number without a claim, or a claim with no source/date. Unsupported: “Retail has no jobs” or “I will get a job.”
“Add the source and report date.” “Name what the 24 counts.” “Change your claim so it only says what the row supports.” Give one precise next step, then retain the learner’s response.

Normal reading, scribing, calculator or typing access does not by itself reduce independence of thought. Record answer prompts separately. Fade prompts without removing normal access. No cold calling or compulsory public performance.

Keep the first claim, support, revised claim and next question in the Careers Portfolio/action plan. Offer to the Communication portfolio. VF verbal feedback; WS supported; I independent; NS next step; // self-edit; ? read back; E actual banked evidence; R after Voice, Audience, NS and learner response in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode.

The scheme outcome and 40-minute sequence are retained. Generic illustrative sets replace named-area/current-data research by owner instruction. Record successful interpretation of the practice sets. Full use of current real-world data would require a separate later application with a checked source; do not claim it here. Week 2 is formative. Week 7 is assessing, with mixed formative/summative source marking retained for Week 6.
Illustrative practice data. All figures and report dates are made up. They do not describe real work or real places.
Fictional report date: 2 November 2026. Unit: advert records. Each column covers 28 days.
The same made-up collection was checked in each window. Each advert record was counted once per window. It does not include all jobs. The numbers do not show who got a job.
Point to construction. Read the count in each window. Has it gone up, down or stayed the same? What can you safely say?
Source and date tell us where and when. The column label tells us the time counted. Keep both in your record.
Latest means the most recent window in this set. These dates do not turn made-up figures into real facts.
Illustrative practice data. All figures and report dates are made up. They do not describe real work or real places.
Fictional report date: 2 November 2026. Unit: total posts in a different made-up set.
Each sector starts at 100 posts for this task. A post is a place for a worker. It may already have a worker in it. This is not a list of jobs to apply for.
A forecast is a prediction. This model assumes the made-up service and spending plans stay the same. If plans change, the forecast can change.
Construction has a forecast of 104 posts. Does this mean four more posts are certain? Explain your view.
A counts advert records. B counts total posts. Do not add their numbers or treat them as the same kind of count.
A model and your next step
Model: health and care in source A
Practice source A has a report date of 2 November 2026. It counts advert records in two 28-day windows.
The count goes from 12 to 18. That is six more records. In this set, more care adverts were counted in October.
This does not prove I would get a care job. I would next check which skills the roles ask for.
Choose one sector in A or B. Record the source and report date. Add the time window or future date and what is counted.
Use a number or a comparison to back your view. Give a cautious claim and a limit that fits. Keep one next research question.
You may speak, point, write, type or use a reader or scribe. Plan in any language. Keep your first idea and any change.
Use source A and the retail row. Keep the source page beside this card. An adult can read each choice.
A: Source A, 2 November 2026. B: Source B, 2 November 2026.
A: People hired. B: Advert records.
A: Fewer retail adverts were counted in the later window. B: There are no retail jobs.
A: This set tells us every job. B: It does not tell us who got a job.
A: The tasks or skills asked for. B: Which job I am certain to get.
“My source is ... . Its report date is ... . It counts ... .”
“In this set, ... goes from ... to ... . This may suggest ... .”
“The data cannot tell me ... . My next question is ... .”
You can use your usual aid. Ask for a pause if you need one. No public answer is needed.
Keep this page apart from first choices. An adult answer is not the learner’s own evidence.
A: Fewer retail adverts in the later window.
B: It does not tell us who got a job.
A: Tasks or skills asked for.
The retail count falls by six. A small set and two short windows do not show all work. The learner can still say what this row shows.
Keep the learner’s source/date choice, numbers and claim. Record any help that supplied an answer. Usual access aids are separate from answer help. Ask what the claim cannot tell us.
Facts or numbers used to help us think. This pack uses made-up numbers.
When a source says it was made or shared.
The time a set of numbers covers.
What a number counts or measures.
A notice about a role. It does not show who got the job.

Something a model takes as true. It may change.
A view that fits the evidence and says what is uncertain.
Something the data cannot tell us.
In this set ... . The count is ... . This may suggest ... . It cannot tell me ... . I would next check ... .
Read, point, speak, write, type or use your normal aid. Plan in any language. You may respond privately.
